introduction_markdown: Time allowed: two and a half hours. Answer ALL questions. Section I is designed to be answered in 1 hour and Section II in 1 1/2 hours; you are advised to divide your time accordingly. In Section II answer EITHER the a, b and c OR the d, e and f of each question. For your guidance the approximate mark(s) for each part of a question is indicated in brackets. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. In calculations you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage. Where necessary, assume: the acceleration of free fall, $g = 10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$; the speed of light in air, $c = 3\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the charge on an electron, $e = 1.6\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$. Non-programmable calculators are allowed.

Table 1 shows the three kinds of radiations emitted during a radioactive decay.

| Radiation | Range in air | Deflection in an electric field | Minimum stopping material |
|---|---|---|---|
| Alpha | | Towards the negative plate | |
| Beta | Few metres | | |
| Gamma | | | Thick sheet of lead |

*Table 1*

(i) Define radioactive decay. *[1 mark]*

(ii) Copy and complete table 1 to identify the different radiations. *[6 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) Radioactive decay is the **spontaneous disintegration of an unstable nucleus, with the emission of radiation** (alpha particles, beta particles or gamma rays), to become more stable.

(ii) Completed table (entries in bold are the ones to add):

| Radiation | Range in air | Deflection in an electric field | Minimum stopping material |
|---|---|---|---|
| Alpha | **A few centimetres (about 5 cm)** | Towards the negative plate | **A thin sheet of paper** |
| Beta | Few metres | **Towards the positive plate** | **A few millimetres of aluminium** |
| Gamma | **Very long (hundreds of metres, almost unlimited)** | **Not deflected** | Thick sheet of lead |

questions.enonce_markdown:
The count rate of a sample of carbon-14, $^{14}_{6}\mathrm{C}$, drops from $1000\,\mathrm{counts\,min^{-1}}$ to $250\,\mathrm{counts\,min^{-1}}$ in $11600$ years.

(i) Define half-life. *[1 mark]*

Determine:

(ii) the half-life of the sample. *[2 marks]*

(iii) the number of protons and neutrons in the carbon nucleus. *[2 marks]*

(iv) the neutron to proton ratio of $^{14}_{6}\mathrm{C}$ and state if it is stable or not. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) The half-life is the **time taken for the count rate (activity) of a radioactive sample to fall to half of its initial value**, equivalently the time for half of the radioactive nuclei in the sample to decay.

(ii) $1000 \xrightarrow{\;T\;} 500 \xrightarrow{\;T\;} 250$: the count rate halves **twice**, so $2T = 11\,600$ years and

$T = \dfrac{11\,600}{2} = 5800$ years.

**The half-life is 5800 years.**

(iii) The atomic number is $6$, so there are **6 protons**; the mass number is $14$, so the number of neutrons is $14 - 6 = $ **8 neutrons**.

(iv) Neutron to proton ratio $= \dfrac{8}{6} = \dfrac{4}{3} \approx 1.33$.

Light stable nuclei have a ratio close to $1$ (for example carbon-12, $6/6$). A ratio above $1$ means there are too many neutrons, so carbon-14 is **not stable**: it is radioactive (it decays by beta emission).

questions.enonce_markdown:
During an earth quake disaster in a certain city, a radioactive isotope with a long half-life escaped from a nuclear power station into the environment.

(i) State two possible health hazards that this could have on the population. *[2 marks]*

(ii) State and explain if after a few weeks, these escaped isotopes could still be hazardous to the population. *[3 marks]*

(iii) State an instrument that can be used to detect the presence of radioactive radiations in the environment. *[1 mark]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) Any two of: **cancer** (for example leukaemia); **radiation burns** or skin damage; **radiation sickness** (nausea, hair loss); **genetic mutations** leading to birth defects in later generations; damage to cells and tissues.

(ii) **Yes, they would still be hazardous.** An isotope with a **long half-life** decays very slowly, so after a few weeks its activity has hardly decreased (only a tiny fraction of the nuclei has decayed) and it keeps emitting dangerous radiation at nearly the same rate for a very long time.

(iii) A **Geiger-Muller (G-M) tube with a counter (ratemeter)**.

questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) **Energy can neither be created nor destroyed**; it can only be **changed from one form to another**, so the total energy of an isolated system remains constant.

questions.enonce_markdown:
An electric motor connected to a pulley system is used to lift a load of $600\,\mathrm{N}$ through a height of $5\,\mathrm{m}$ in $6\,\mathrm{s}$. A current of $3\,\mathrm{A}$ flows through the motor when it is connected to a $220\,\mathrm{V}$ supply.

(i) Define power. *[1 mark]*

(ii) Determine the energy supplied to the motor. *[2 marks]*

(iii) Determine the work done in lifting the load. *[2 marks]*

(iv) Explain whether or not the motor is 100 % efficient. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) Power is the **rate of doing work (or of transferring energy)**, $P = \dfrac{W}{t}$. Unit: watt (W), $1\,\mathrm{W} = 1\,\mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}$.

(ii) Energy supplied to the motor $E = VIt = 220\times3\times6 = 3960\,\mathrm{J}$.

**The energy supplied is $3960\,\mathrm{J}$** ($\approx 4.0\times10^{3}\,\mathrm{J}$).

(iii) Work done in lifting the load $W = Fh = 600\times5 = 3000\,\mathrm{J}$.

**The work done is $3000\,\mathrm{J}$.**

(iv) **The motor is not 100 % efficient.** The useful work output ($3000\,\mathrm{J}$) is less than the energy supplied ($3960\,\mathrm{J}$): efficiency $= \dfrac{3000}{3960}\times100 \approx 76\,\%$. The remaining $960\,\mathrm{J}$ is wasted as **heat** (resistance of the windings), **friction** in the pulley and bearings, and **sound**.

questions.enonce_markdown:
A hydro-electric power plant derives its power from a dam built $75\,\mathrm{m}$ above the turbines. $500\,\mathrm{kg}$ of water falls on the turbines every second.

(i) State two hazards that may result from a careless use of electricity. *[2 marks]*

(ii) Calculate the potential energy of the $500\,\mathrm{kg}$ of water from the dam as it starts falling. *[2 marks]*

(iii) Explain why the amount of electricity supply during the dry season is less than during the rainy season. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) Any two of: **electric shock (electrocution)**; **fire** caused by overloaded sockets or short circuits (overheated wires); **burns** from hot or faulty appliances.

(ii) $\mathrm{P.E.} = mgh = 500\times10\times75 = 375\,000\,\mathrm{J} = 3.75\times10^{5}\,\mathrm{J}$.

**The potential energy is $3.75\times10^{5}\,\mathrm{J}$** (released each second, a power of $375\,\mathrm{kW}$).

(iii) In the dry season there is **little rain**, so the **water level in the dam falls** and the flow of water is smaller: less water (and a smaller height of fall) reaches the turbines each second, so **less potential energy is converted** into kinetic energy and then electrical energy. In the rainy season the dam is full and more water flows, so more electricity is produced.
